turns.prompt_text: My Beats Solo 4 have poor audio quality only when on bluetooth with my macbook
turns.response_html:
This is a common issue with Bluetooth headphones (including Apple/Beats products like the Solo 4) when paired with a Mac. The poor audio quality is usually caused by the Mac switching the headphones to a lower-quality audio profile when it detects the microphone is being used.

Here are the most likely causes and solutions, drawing from similar experiences with Beats and other Bluetooth headphones on macOS:

1. Microphone Usage Downgrading Audio Quality (Most Common)

When you use your Beats Solo 4 on Bluetooth, the connection operates in two different modes:

  • High-Quality Audio (A2DP): For listening only, using a higher quality codec (like AAC or a high-bitrate SBC) and sample rate (e.g., 44.1 kHz or 48 kHz).
  • Headset/Calling Mode (HFP/HSP): For simultaneous listening and speaking (using the built-in microphone). To manage both streams over limited Bluetooth bandwidth, the audio quality switches to a much lower sample rate (often 8 kHz or 16 kHz) and lower-quality codec (like SBC or mSBC), resulting in that "tinny" or "AM radio" sound.

Potential Fixes:

  • Check for Active Microphones: The downgrade can be triggered by any application that has access to and is actively monitoring the microphone, even if you aren't on a call. This includes:

    • Video conferencing apps (Zoom, Teams, etc.)
    • Voice chat apps (Discord, Slack)
    • Siri
    • Voice recording or dictation apps
    • Even the Sound settings or Audio MIDI Setup window being open on your Mac can sometimes activate the mic.
    • Solution: Quit any of these apps completely, then try playing audio again.

  • Manually Switch Input Device: You can force your Mac to use its built-in microphone instead of the Beats Solo 4's microphone, which should leave the headphones in high-quality audio output mode.

    1. Open System Settings (or System Preferences on older macOS versions).
    2. Go to Sound.
    3. Select the Input tab.
    4. Change the input device from your Beats Solo 4 to the MacBook Pro Microphone or Internal Microphone.
    5. Check the Output tab to ensure your Beats Solo 4 are still selected for sound output.

2. General Bluetooth Troubleshooting

If the microphone issue is not the cause, you can try resetting or re-establishing the Bluetooth connection:

  • Reset the Connection:
    1. Go to System Settings > Bluetooth.
    2. Find your Beats Solo 4 in the list, click the 'i' or Options button, and select Forget Device (or Remove).
    3. Turn Bluetooth off on your Mac, then restart your Mac.
    4. After the restart, turn Bluetooth back on and re-pair your Beats Solo 4.
  • Check Audio MIDI Setup: In the Audio MIDI Setup app (found in the Utilities folder), select your Beats Solo 4. Make sure the output format is set to a higher sample rate (e.g., 44.1 kHz or 48 kHz) and not 8 kHz or 16 kHz.

3. Bluetooth Codec Issue

Macs primarily use AAC or SBC codecs for audio. If the Mac is defaulting to the lower-quality SBC codec, it can affect sound quality. Since the Solo 4 are an Apple product, they should default to AAC, but sometimes a glitch can cause a fallback.

  • Check Active Codec: You can check the active codec by holding down the Option (Alt) key and clicking the Bluetooth icon in your menu bar. Hover over your Beats Solo 4; the Active Codec should display. If it says SBC, it might be the cause, though this is less common with Apple's own Beats headphones.

turns.prompt_text: How can I deactivate the mic when on the macbook?
turns.response_html:
That's a great question, as controlling which microphone your Mac uses is the key to maintaining high-fidelity audio (the A2DP profile) on your Beats Solo 4.

The goal is to force your Mac to use its Internal Microphone and completely ignore the microphone built into your Beats Solo 4, preventing the Mac from switching to the poor-quality Headset (HSP/HFP) profile.

Here are the most effective methods, from simplest to a permanent fix:

1. The Quick Manual Switch (Temporary Fix)

This is the fastest way to fix the audio if it degrades mid-stream, but you may have to repeat it every time an app activates the mic.

  1. Hold the Option Key ($\text{⌥}$): Press and hold the Option key on your keyboard.
  2. Click the Volume Icon: Click the Volume icon ($\text{🔊}$) in your Mac's menu bar (or click the Control Center icon and then the volume control).
  3. Change the Input Device: Under the "Input" section, select MacBook Pro Microphone (or Internal Microphone) instead of your Beats Solo 4.

The moment you switch the input source away from the Beats, the headphones should immediately revert to the high-quality A2DP audio profile for playback.

2. Set the Default Input in System Settings (Semi-Permanent)

This method often works to prevent the mic from switching back, especially when you connect the headphones.

  1. Go to System Settings (or System Preferences).
  2. Click Sound.
  3. Select the Input tab.
  4. Explicitly select your MacBook Pro Microphone (or Internal Microphone) as the input device.

As long as you leave this setting alone, it should prioritize the internal mic over the Beats mic. If the audio still degrades, check if a specific application (like Zoom, Discord, etc.) is overriding this setting.

3. Create an Aggregate Device (Most Permanent Solution)

This method uses a built-in macOS utility to essentially "lock" the Mac into using the internal mic, making it the most reliable solution for permanently deactivating the Bluetooth mic for system-wide use.

  1. Open Audio MIDI Setup: Press Command + Spacebar ($\text{⌘}+\text{Space}$) to open Spotlight Search, then type "Audio MIDI Setup" and open the application (it's in the Utilities folder).
  2. Create a New Device: In the Audio Devices window, click the + button in the bottom-left corner and select Create Aggregate Device.
  3. Select the Internal Mic: On the right-hand side, check the box next to your Built-in Microphone (or MacBook Pro Microphone). Crucially, ensure you do NOT select your Beats Solo 4 as a component.
  4. Set the Default Input: You can double-click the new device and rename it (e.g., "Locked Internal Mic"). Then, right-click (or Control-click) on this new Aggregate Device and select Use This Device for Sound Input.

Now, your Mac's default audio input is this new locked device, which only includes your internal microphone. This prevents the Mac from automatically switching the input to your Beats, keeping your Beats Solo 4 in the high-quality A2DP output mode.
